inference_aids.alt: Freyja weeps tears of red gold in her chariot drawn by two cats.
inference_aids.art_brief: Black ink woodcut with restrained red-gold accents, in the established Kvöldvakan myth style. A composite of s057 and s061 in afi’s retelling: Freyja, fully clothed in a plain long gown, sits alone in a small chariot drawn by exactly two cats; tears fall from her face and turn into drops of red gold below. The chariot and cats come from Gylfaginning 24, the golden tears for the absent Óður from chapter 35; this combines source motifs rather than claiming a single narrated journey. No Óður or daughter is present, no reunion, no additional cats. A spare distant landscape, no lettering. Planned only; all word meanings are carried by the prose and local aids.

cover.art_brief: Ink and watercolour in the established Kvöldvakan farm style. Hamrar, late May 1876, the light northern evening immediately continuing Kafli 18. words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Helga sagði: „Mig langar vestur.“ Hjartað hennar var hálft hér og hálft fyrir vestan. Í draumnum sá hún fjöllin heima frá skipinu. Svo sá hún þau ekki. Hún var glöð í draumnum, en heima grét hún.
Freyja grét af þrá. Hún saknaði Óðs. Hann fór langar leiðir, og hún leitaði að honum. Tár hennar voru úr rauðu gulli.
Guðrún horfði á Helgu. Hún kveið sumrinu, en hún trúði dóttur sinni. Hún nefndi ekki sína þrá. Hún valdi sögu um Freyju og Óð.
words_with_history.note_en: Þrá is the noun “longing”; the verb þrá, “to long for”, has the same citation form but is not introduced as a second lexeme here. Guðrún’s unnamed longing is a reading of her choice of story, not a statement by Snorri.

grammar.title: Mig langar, mér finnst
grammar.rule: „Mig langar vestur.“ · „Mér finnst langt til Ameríku.“ · „Líður þér illa?“

tables.caption: nútíð · þátíð
rows: Mig langar vestur · Mig langaði þangað allan veturinn (s003)
Stundum dreymir mig sama drauminn (s020) · Mig dreymdi Óla í nótt (s034)
Mér líður illa (s018) · henni leið illa (s015)

grammar.note_en:
An oblique subject is the person experiencing a feeling or need expressed in a case other than the nominative. The nominative is the ordinary subject form ég, “I”; accusative mig and dative mér both refer to the same speaker here. The verb determines which case is used. The case does not mean that this person has become the object of an ordinary personal verb. Learn the expression together with its case.

Langa, vanta and dreyma take an accusative experiencer: Mig langar vestur (s003), “I want / long to go west”, literally “me (accusative) longs west”; Mig vantar framtíð (s005), “I need a future”; Stundum dreymir mig sama drauminn (s020), “Sometimes I dream the same dream”. The thing lacking or dreamt about is separate from the experiencer. Hvað vantar þig hér? (s004) means “What do you lack here?” Þig is the accusative “you”. Nú vantar okkur hjú (s030) means “Now we need farm servants”. Okkur is accusative here, although accusative and dative have the same form okkur. Vanta does not become a dative-subject verb in that sentence.

Finnast, líka, þykja, líða and lítast á take a dative experiencer in these examples. Mér finnst langt til Ameríku (s025) means “I think it is a long way to America”, literally “to me (dative) it seems far to America”. Mér líkar ekki þessi Ameríka (s040) means “I do not like this America”. Líkar is the verb “like”; líka in “Jón og Sólveig fara líka” (s010), “Jón and Sólveig are going too”, is the adverb “also”. Mér þykir þetta falleg saga (s073) means “I think this is a beautiful story”. Mér líður illa (s018) means “I feel bad”. Mér er kalt (s032) means “I am cold”, literally “to me is cold”. Mér líst ekki á það (s002) means “I do not like the look of it”. Lítast á expresses an impression of something; its present form here is líst, with á before the thing being judged. Finna and líta as ordinary personal verbs have other uses; these expressions are learned together, without generalising their -st forms to new verbs.

Mér finnst margt, Helga (s049) means “I feel/think many things, Helga”. Guðrún leaves those thoughts unnamed: she will not say what she thinks. 

The finite verb is third-person singular in every oblique-subject frame shown here, whether the experiencer is mig, þig, henni or plural okkur. A finite verb is the part carrying tense: langar, dreymir, vantar, líður or er. Do not change langar to a first-person form because the meaning is “I want”. This rule describes the frames in this chapter, not every possible Icelandic construction containing a dative phrase.

The experiencer need not be the first word. Stundum dreymir mig sama drauminn (s020), “Sometimes I dream the same dream”, puts the finite verb after the initial adverb. In the question Langar þig líka, mamma? (s046), “Do you want to as well, Mum?”, the verb precedes the accusative experiencer. Hvað vantar þig hér? (s004), “What do you lack here?”, begins with the question word, then the verb and þig. Hvað finnst þér? (s024), “What do you think?”, has the same order with dative þér. Líður þér illa? (s017) means “Do you feel bad?” The negator ekki follows the finite verb in Mér líst ekki á það (s002), “I do not like the look of it”.

Mig langar að plus an infinitive expresses a wanted action. An infinitive is the naming form of the verb. Mig langar að heyra sögu (s054) means “I want to hear a story”. Mig langar ekki að kveðja ykkur (s023) means “I do not want to say goodbye to you”. Keep að before the infinitive heyra or kveðja. Vestur in Mig langar vestur (s003), “I want to go west”, is instead a direction, so there is no að before it.

The past does not change the required subject case. Mig langaði þangað allan veturinn (s003) means “I wanted to go there all winter”; langar becomes langaði. Mig dreymdi Óla í nótt (s034) means “I dreamt about Óli last night”; dreymir becomes dreymdi. Henni leið illa (s015) means “She felt bad”: henni is dative “she”, referring to Helga, and leið is the strong past of líða. Compare present Mér líður illa (s018), “I feel bad”. Only these past pairs are tabulated here; fannst, þótti, leist and vantaði are not story forms in this chapter and are not production targets.

Ásta says Mér langar líka vestur (s044), “I want to go west too”, using dative mér where standard Icelandic uses accusative mig. This widespread spoken substitution is called þágufallssýki (“dative sickness”); it is common in speech but non-standard in this frame. Guðrún corrects her with Mig langar, Ásta mín (s045), “‘I want’ is mig langar, my Ásta”, and Ásta repeats the standard form in s046. The non-standard example belongs only to Ásta’s speech and recognition work. Production answers use mig langar. These tables consolidate this chapter alone; the end-of-part cumulative table belongs in Kafli 20.
